{{Short description|Governance of the Northwest Territories}}
{{Expand French|topic=gov|Politique au Nunavut|date=March 2026}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=May 2026}}
[[File:Coat of arms of Nunavut.svg|thumb|right|[[Coat of arms of Nunavut]]]]
The '''politics of the Nunavut''' involves not only the governance of the [[Nunavut]] but also the social, economic and political issues specific to the [[Provinces and territories of Canada|territory]]. This includes matters relating to local governance and governance by the [[Government of Canada|federal government]] of [[Canada]], the inclusion of the [[Aboriginal peoples in Canada|aboriginal]] population in territorial affairs, and the matter of official languages for the territory.

== History ==
Key to the politics and governance of Nunavut are the limits on the jurisdiction of the territorial government. Territories of Canada have no [[inherent jurisdiction]] and only have those powers [[Devolution|devolved]] to them by the federal government.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Northwest Territories Act|year=1985 |url=http://laws.justice.gc.ca/en/N-27/252179.html |author=Department of Justice Canada|access-date=January 27, 2007}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://laws.justice.gc.ca/en/Y-2.01/265655.html|title=Yukon Act|year=2002|author=Department of Justice Canada|access-date=January 27, 2007}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://laws.justice.gc.ca/en/N-28.6/index.html|title=Nunavut Act|year=1993|author=Department of Justice Canada|access-date=January 27, 2007}}</ref> The devolution and delegation of power to the territory has always been a factor in the territory's politics. On January 18, 2024, the federal and territorial governments signed the Nunavut Lands and Resources Devolution Agreement; it gives the government of Nunavut control over the territory's land and resources.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-17 |title=Government of Canada, Government of Nunavut, and Nunavut Tunngavik Incorporated reach final agreement on the devolution of Nunavut |url=https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2024/01/18/government-canada-government-nunavut-nunavut-tunngavik |access-date=2026-06-11 |website=Prime Minister of Canada |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Tranter |first=Emma |date=18 January 2024 |title='It's high time': Nunavut officially takes over land, resource responsibilities from feds |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/nunavut-trudeau-sign-devolution-argreement-1.7086272 |work=[[CBC News]] |access-date=4 April 2026}}</ref>

A hallmark of politics in Nunavut is that it operates as under a “[[Consensus government in Canada|consensus government]]” system.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=2021-11-17 |title=Nunavut assembly to choose premier, cabinet in secret ballot vote |url=https://lethbridgenewsnow.com/2021/11/17/nunavut-assembly-to-choose-premier-cabinet-in-secret-ballot-vote/ |access-date=2025-03-20 |work=Lethbridge News Now}}</ref> Candidates for election to the territorial legislature do not stand as members of a [[List of political parties in Canada|political party]].<ref name=":0" /> While some candidates may express an affiliation or membership with a party, party membership is not recognized in the legislature.<ref name=":0" /> As a result, the [[Member of the Legislative Assembly|Members of the Legislative Assembly]] select a [[Premier of the Northwest Territories|Premier]] by way of a [[secret ballot]], rather than on the basis of party affiliation (see [[Responsible government]]).<ref name=":0" />

Local governance has been a long-standing issue in the territory. This includes not only the loss of local government authority from the period from 1905 to 1951, when Ottawa asserted direct control over the governance of the [[Northwest Territories]], but also related matters of aboriginal self-governance and land claims.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bartlett |first=Richard |date=1978-10-01 |title=The Indian Act of Canada |url=https://digitalcommons.law.buffalo.edu/buffalolawreview/vol27/iss4/3/ |journal=Buffalo Law Review |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=581 |issn=0023-9356}}</ref> This latter issue lead, in part, to the division of the former Northwest Territories into the present Northwest Territories and Nunavut.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dacks |first=Gurston |date=1986 |title=The Case against Dividing the Northwest Territories |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3550729 |journal=Canadian Public Policy / Analyse de Politiques |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=202–213 |doi=10.2307/3550729 |jstor=3550729 |issn=0317-0861|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Abele |first1=Frances |last2=Dickerson |first2=Mark O. |date=1985 |title=The 1982 Plebiscite on Division of the Northwest Territories: Regional Government and Federal Policy |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3550376 |journal=Canadian Public Policy / Analyse de Politiques |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=1–15 |doi=10.2307/3550376 |jstor=3550376 |issn=0317-0861|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Légaré |first=André |date=2008-09-01 |title=Inuit identity and regionalization in the Canadian Central and Eastern Arctic: a survey of writings about Nunavut |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10889370701742845 |journal=Polar Geography |volume=31 |issue=3–4 |pages=99–118 |doi=10.1080/10889370701742845 |issn=1088-937X}}</ref>

== Federal language ==
Language has also been a long-standing issue in Nunavut politics. [[French language|French]] became an official language, along with [[English language|English]], in 1877.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Aunger |first=Edmund A. |date=1998 |title=The Mystery of the French Language Ordinances: An Investigation into Official Bilingualism and the Canadian North-West—1870 to 1895 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0829320100005597/type/journal_article |journal=Canadian Journal of Law and Society |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=89–124 |doi=10.1017/S0829320100005597 |issn=0829-3201|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Under Official Languages Act, which became law in 2013, and the Inuit Language Protection Act, which became law in 2008, the official languages of the territory are English, French, Inuktitut, and Inuinnaqtun.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tranter |first=Emma |date=2023-10-01 |title=Nunavut reviewing its language laws for the 1st time |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/nunavut-looks-to-review-its-language-laws-for-the-first-time-1.6982953 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240830184921/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/nunavut-looks-to-review-its-language-laws-for-the-first-time-1.6982953 |archive-date=2024-08-30 |access-date=2025-03-20 |work=CBC News}}</ref>
